# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The invention is a reusable hand tool that locates and guides two drill holes for a cabinet pull without requiring a powered measuring system. The tool has an elongated straight rail with a flat lower face that rests on the front face of a cabinet door or drawer front. A straight longitudinal slot runs through the rail. Distance marks are printed along the upper face beside the slot.

A fixed fence is attached at the first end of the rail. The fence extends downward from the lower face and bears against one straight edge of the workpiece. The fence is perpendicular to the rail, so the rail extends inward across the workpiece when the fence bears against the edge. A removable spacer plate can be fitted between the fence and the workpiece edge. The spacer plate has parallel opposite faces and changes the setback of every guided hole by its thickness without changing the separation between the holes.

Two separate guide carriages sit on the upper face of the rail. Each carriage has a lower key that passes into the longitudinal slot, and the key prevents the carriage from rotating while allowing it to slide along the slot. Each carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing with a vertical bore. The bore passes completely through the carriage and aligns with an opening through the slot so a drill bit can reach the workpiece. The two bushing axes are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face of the rail.

Each carriage has a threaded clamp knob above the rail. A threaded shank of the knob passes through the carriage and the longitudinal slot into a clamping shoe below the rail. Turning the knob draws the shoe toward the carriage and clamps the rail between the carriage and the shoe. Loosening the knob allows the carriage to slide. The first carriage has a pointer aligned with its bushing axis and readable against the distance marks. The second carriage has its own pointer aligned with its bushing axis. The difference between the two pointer readings is therefore the center-to-center hole spacing.

The rail has a transverse center index at its midpoint. A shallow V-shaped sight notch is formed in the second end of the rail and aligned with the center index. The user can align the center index and the sight notch with a pencil centerline on the workpiece before tightening both carriage knobs. The fence controls setback from the workpiece edge, while the two pointer readings control hole separation and the position of the pair relative to the centerline.

The fence is reversible. It is secured to the first end of the rail by two screws received in two corresponding holes. Removing the screws, turning the fence over, and reinstalling the screws moves the downwardly projecting part of the fence from one longitudinal side of the rail to the opposite longitudinal side. This lets the same marked upper face be used when the tool is referenced from either an upper edge or a lower edge of a workpiece.

To use the tool, the user selects the desired hole spacing, loosens both clamp knobs, slides the carriages until their pointer readings have the desired difference and are centered about the transverse center index, and tightens the knobs. The user places the lower face on the workpiece, presses the fence or the installed spacer plate against the selected workpiece edge, aligns the sight notch and center index with the pencil centerline, and drills through both bushings. The tool is then lifted away. No part remains attached to the workpiece.

The rail, fence, carriage bodies, shoes, spacer plate, pointers, and knobs may be made from rigid polymer or metal. The drill bushings are replaceable wear parts and are made from hardened metal. The tool has no motor, battery, electronic sensor, or network connection.

The fence 30 is a fixed fence in the sense that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and does not slide along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below do. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92, as shown in FIG. 4. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90 at a right angle to that edge. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.
8	
9	Referring to FIG. 6, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.
10	
11	The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed, so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes.
12	
13	A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 is fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.
14	
15	Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are seated separately on the rail 10, one nearer to the fence 30 than the other. The two guide carriages are separate bodies. Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.
16	
17	The construction of the guide carriages is shown in FIG. 3, a cross-sectional view taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 2. The view shows the second guide carriage 70; the first guide carriage 50 is of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key 52 (FIG. 3) that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.
18	
19	Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing 54 (FIG. 3). The drill bushing 54 has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down the bore of the drill bushing 54 travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.
20	
21	The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore has been enlarged by use, or whose bore is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.
22	
23	Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 (FIG. 1) above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 (FIG. 3) below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 remains below the lower face 14 and spans the longitudinal slot 16, so that it bears against the lower face 14 on each side of the longitudinal slot 16 when the clamp knob 58 is tightened and travels with the guide carriage along the rail 10 when the clamp knob 58 is loosened.
24	
25	The first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82, as seen in FIG. 2. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is an index feature that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.
26	
27	Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.
28	
29	Referring to FIG. 2, the rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the rail 10 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 (FIG. 2) is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, so that a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 2) drawn on the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90. Sighting the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 together on the centerline 94 brings both of those features onto the centerline 94, and the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are spaced apart along the rail 10 so that the two sightings together fix the position of the jig on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92.
30	
31	The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.
32	
33	In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. Both clamp knobs 58 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.
34	
35	The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.
36	
37	When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.
38	
39	The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoes 60, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knobs 58 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushings 54 are made of hardened metal. The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed features.
40	
41	The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and it requires no power source of any kind. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.
42	
43	The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and downward refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece that is held vertically or horizontally for drilling. These terms are used for convenience of description and do not limit the orientation in which the jig may be used.

Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 3). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 (FIG. 2) are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.

The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door, a drawer front, or a like panel having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes that receive the mounting screws of a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.

A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 is a fixed fence in the sense that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and does not slide along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below do. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92, as shown in FIG. 4. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90 at a right angle to that edge. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.

Referring to FIG. 6, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.

The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed, so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes.

A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 is fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.

Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are seated separately on the rail 10, one nearer to the fence 30 than the other. The two guide carriages are separate bodies. Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.

The construction of the guide carriages is shown in FIG. 3, a cross-sectional view taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 2. The view shows the second guide carriage 70; the first guide carriage 50 is of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key 52 (FIG. 3) that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.

Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing 54 (FIG. 3). The drill bushing 54 has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down the bore of the drill bushing 54 travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.

The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore has been enlarged by use, or whose bore is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 (FIG. 1) above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 (FIG. 3) below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 remains below the lower face 14 and spans the longitudinal slot 16, so that it bears against the lower face 14 on each side of the longitudinal slot 16 when the clamp knob 58 is tightened and travels with the guide carriage along the rail 10 when the clamp knob 58 is loosened.

The first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82, as seen in FIG. 2. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is an index feature that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.

Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.

Referring to FIG. 2, the rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the rail 10 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 (FIG. 2) is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, so that a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 2) drawn on the workpiece 90 is visible in the sight notch 26 when the jig is placed on the workpiece 90. Sighting the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 together on the centerline 94 brings both of those features onto the centerline 94, and the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are spaced apart along the rail 10 so that the two sightings together fix the position of the jig on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92.

The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.

In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. Both clamp knobs 58 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. Both clamp knobs 58 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.

The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, no fastener is driven into the workpiece 90 to hold the jig, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.

When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.

The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoes 60, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knobs 58 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushings 54 are made of hardened metal. The distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the pointers may be printed features.

The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and it requires no power source of any kind. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The rail 10 may be of any length sufficient to span the pull patterns to be drilled, the distance marks 18 may be graduated in any convenient unit, and the drill bushings 54 may be provided in a set of bore diameters. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

1. A drilling jig for locating and guiding a pair of holes in a workpiece having a front face and a straight edge, the drilling jig comprising:

an elongated straight rail having a flat lower face for resting on the front face, an upper face, a first end, a second end, a first longitudinal side, a second longitudinal side opposite the first longitudinal side, and a longitudinal slot extending through the rail from the upper face to the lower face, the upper face carrying distance marks alongside the longitudinal slot;

a fence releasably secured to the first end of the rail by two screws received in two corresponding mounting holes, the fence having a downwardly projecting portion that extends below the lower face and that is perpendicular to the rail for bearing against the straight edge, the fence being securable to the first end of the rail in a first orientation in which the downwardly projecting portion lies on the first longitudinal side of the rail and, upon removal of the two screws, inversion of the fence, and reinstallation of the two screws in the same two mounting holes, in a second orientation in which the downwardly projecting portion lies on the second longitudinal side of the rail, the upper face and the distance marks carried on the upper face facing away from the front face in both the first orientation and the second orientation;

a first guide carriage and a second guide carriage seated separately on the upper face of the rail, each of the first guide carriage and the second guide carriage comprising:

a key depending into the longitudinal slot and bearing against side walls of the longitudinal slot so as to prevent rotation of that guide carriage relative to the rail while permitting that guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot,

a cylindrical drill bushing having a bore that passes completely through that guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot, and

a clamp knob above the rail, the clamp knob having a threaded shank that passes through that guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot into a clamping shoe below the rail, whereby tightening the clamp knob draws the clamping shoe toward that guide carriage and clamps the rail between that guide carriage and the clamping shoe, and loosening the clamp knob permits that guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot;

the bore of the drill bushing of the first guide carriage and the bore of the drill bushing of the second guide carriage being parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face of the rail; and

a first pointer on the first guide carriage, the first pointer being aligned with an axis of the bore of the drill bushing of the first guide carriage and readable against the distance marks, and a second pointer on the second guide carriage, the second pointer being aligned with an axis of the bore of the drill bushing of the second guide carriage and readable against the distance marks.

2. The drilling jig of claim 1, wherein the first guide carriage and the second guide carriage are separate bodies that are uncoupled from one another, each being positionable along the longitudinal slot and clampable to the rail independently of the other.

3. The drilling jig of claim 1, wherein the first pointer and the second pointer are readable against the same distance marks, such that a difference between a reading of the first pointer and a reading of the second pointer is a center-to-center spacing of the pair of holes to be guided by the drilling jig.

4. The drilling jig of claim 1, wherein the rail has a transverse center index at a midpoint of the rail.

5. The drilling jig of claim 4, further comprising a shallow V-shaped sight notch formed in the second end of the rail and aligned with the transverse center index.

6. The drilling jig of claim 5, wherein the sight notch opens through an end edge of the second end of the rail, such that a centerline marked on the front face of the workpiece is visible in the sight notch when the flat lower face rests on the front face, the sight notch and the transverse center index being spaced apart along the rail so as to be sighted together on the centerline.

7. The drilling jig of claim 1, further comprising a removable spacer plate having parallel opposite faces, the spacer plate being fittable between the downwardly projecting portion of the fence and the straight edge of the workpiece so as to increase a setback of both holes of the pair from the straight edge by a thickness of the spacer plate without changing a separation between the holes of the pair.

8. The drilling jig of claim 1, wherein the distance marks read in the same direction along the rail when the fence is in the first orientation and when the fence is in the second orientation.

9. The drilling jig of claim 1, wherein the drill bushing of each of the first guide carriage and the second guide carriage is of hardened metal and is received in a body of that guide carriage as a separate piece that is withdrawable from that guide carriage and replaceable by another drill bushing.

10. The drilling jig of claim 9, wherein the rail, the fence, a body of the first guide carriage, a body of the second guide carriage, the clamping shoe of each guide carriage, the first pointer, the second pointer, and the clamp knob of each guide carriage are of rigid polymer or metal.

11. The drilling jig of claim 1, wherein the drilling jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection, and every setting of the drilling jig is made mechanically and read directly from the distance marks.

12. The drilling jig of claim 1, wherein the clamping shoe of each guide carriage remains below the lower face of the rail and spans the longitudinal slot, so as to bear against the lower face of the rail when the clamp knob of that guide carriage is tightened and to be released from the lower face of the rail when that clamp knob is loosened.

13. A drilling jig for locating and guiding a pair of holes in a workpiece having a front face, a straight edge, and a centerline marked on the front face, the drilling jig comprising:

an elongated straight rail having a flat lower face for resting on the front face, an upper face, a first end, a second end, and a longitudinal slot extending through the rail from the upper face to the lower face, the upper face carrying distance marks alongside the longitudinal slot;

a fixed fence at the first end of the rail, the fixed fence having a downwardly projecting portion that extends below the lower face and that is perpendicular to the rail for bearing against the straight edge, so that the rail extends inward across the front face at a right angle to the straight edge;

a transverse center index on the upper face at a midpoint of the rail, and a shallow V-shaped sight notch formed in the second end of the rail and aligned with the transverse center index, for sighting on the centerline;

a first guide carriage and a second guide carriage seated separately on the upper face of the rail, each of the first guide carriage and the second guide carriage comprising a key depending into the longitudinal slot that prevents rotation of that guide carriage relative to the rail while permitting that guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot, a cylindrical drill bushing having a bore that passes completely through that guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot, and a clamp knob above the rail having a threaded shank that passes through that guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot into a clamping shoe below the rail, whereby tightening the clamp knob clamps the rail between that guide carriage and the clamping shoe; and

a first pointer on the first guide carriage aligned with an axis of the bore of the drill bushing of the first guide carriage and readable against the distance marks, and a second pointer on the second guide carriage aligned with an axis of the bore of the drill bushing of the second guide carriage and readable against the distance marks, whereby the first guide carriage and the second guide carriage are settable to readings that differ by a selected center-to-center hole spacing and that lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index.

14. The drilling jig of claim 13, wherein the bore of the drill bushing of the first guide carriage and the bore of the drill bushing of the second guide carriage are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face of the rail.

15. The drilling jig of claim 13, further comprising a removable spacer plate having parallel opposite faces, the spacer plate being fittable between the downwardly projecting portion of the fixed fence and the straight edge of the workpiece so as to increase a setback of both holes of the pair from the straight edge by a thickness of the spacer plate without changing a separation between the holes of the pair.

loosening the clamp knob of the first guide carriage and the clamp knob of the second guide carriage;

sliding the first guide carriage and the second guide carriage along the longitudinal slot until a difference between a reading of the pointer of the first guide carriage against the distance marks and a reading of the pointer of the second guide carriage against the distance marks equals a selected center-to-center hole spacing, and until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index;

moving the drilling jig along the straight edge until the transverse center index and the sight notch are aligned with the centerline;

drilling through the drill bushing of the first guide carriage and through the drill bushing of the second guide carriage into the workpiece; and

lifting the drilling jig away from the workpiece, no part of the drilling jig remaining attached to the workpiece.

==> draft/04-field.md <==
The present disclosure relates to hand tools for woodworking and cabinet installation, and more particularly to a reusable jig that both locates and guides the pair of drilled holes required to mount a cabinet pull on a door or a drawer front.

==> draft/05-background.md <==
Mounting a pull on a cabinet door or a drawer front requires two holes that satisfy three separate conditions at once. The two holes must lie at a common setback from a straight edge of the workpiece, they must be separated by the center-to-center spacing of the particular pull being installed, and the pair must sit symmetrically about a chosen centerline of the workpiece. A hole that is correct in one of these three respects and wrong in another still spoils a finished panel, and a panel that has been drilled cannot be corrected by moving the hole.

Laying the holes out by hand with a rule and a square requires the installer to compute and mark two positions for every panel, to transfer each mark accurately, and then to start a drill bit exactly on a pencil intersection on a hard and often prefinished surface. Small errors in measuring, in marking, and in bit wander accumulate independently on each of the two holes, so the pair can be out of square with the edge even when each individual measurement was made carefully. Repeating the layout on every door and drawer front of a run multiplies both the labor and the opportunities for error.

Simple drilling guides reduce part of this burden by presenting a hardened bushing that both positions the bit and keeps it perpendicular to the surface. A guide of that kind still leaves the installer to establish where the guide itself is placed on the panel, and a guide that fixes the two bushings at a single separation serves only one pull pattern. Adjustable arrangements in which a scale is read once and a second hole is measured from the first reintroduce the accumulation of error that the guide was meant to remove, because an error in setting the single reading displaces both holes and an error in transferring the spacing displaces only one of them.

A further difficulty arises from the direction in which the workpiece is referenced. A pull on an upper cabinet door is commonly located from the lower edge of the door, while a pull on a drawer front or a base cabinet door is commonly located from the upper edge or from a stile edge on the opposite side. A jig whose edge fence projects from one longitudinal side of its body can be referenced from the opposite edge only by turning the whole jig over, which puts the marked and readable face of the jig against the panel where it cannot be seen, or by printing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which invites the installer to read the wrong scale. Neither expedient is satisfactory in the field, where the installer moves repeatedly between doors and drawer fronts on the same run of cabinets.

Powered and electronically assisted layout systems can measure and record positions, but they add cost, require charging or batteries, and are unnecessary for an operation whose entire geometry is fixed by one straight edge, one centerline, and one spacing dimension.

==> draft/06-summary.md <==
A drilling jig is disclosed that locates and guides both holes of a cabinet pull pattern in a single placement of a hand tool, without any powered measuring system.

The jig includes an elongated straight rail having a flat lower face that rests on the front face of a cabinet door or drawer front, an upper face, and a straight longitudinal slot extending through the rail from the upper face to the lower face. Distance marks are carried on the upper face alongside the longitudinal slot.

A fence is secured to a first end of the rail by two screws received in two corresponding holes. The fence has a portion that projects below the lower face and bears against a straight edge of the workpiece, and the fence is perpendicular to the rail so that the rail extends inward across the workpiece while the projecting portion bears against the edge. The fence is reversible. Removing the two screws, turning the fence over, and reinstalling the two screws moves the projecting portion from one longitudinal side of the rail to the opposite longitudinal side, while the marked upper face continues to face away from the workpiece. The same face of the rail, carrying the same distance marks reading in the same direction, is therefore used whether the tool is referenced from an upper edge or a lower edge of the workpiece, and the installer never has to read a second scale or work from an inverted tool.

Two separate guide carriages are seated on the upper face of the rail. Each guide carriage has a lower key that passes into the longitudinal slot, and the key prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot. Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing having a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot, so that a drill bit passed through the bore reaches the workpiece. The two bores are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face of the rail.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob above the rail. A threaded shank of the clamp knob passes through the guide carriage and the longitudinal slot into a clamping shoe below the rail. Turning the clamp knob draws the clamping shoe toward the guide carriage and clamps the rail between the guide carriage and the clamping shoe. Loosening the clamp knob allows the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot.

The first guide carriage carries a first pointer aligned with the axis of its bore and readable against the distance marks, and the second guide carriage carries a second pointer aligned with the axis of its bore and readable against the distance marks. Each hole of the pair is therefore set by its own reading taken directly from the same scale, and the difference between the two pointer readings is the center-to-center hole spacing. An error made in setting one guide carriage does not propagate into the position of the other.

The rail has a transverse center index at its midpoint, and a shallow V-shaped sight notch is formed in a second end of the rail and aligned with the transverse center index. The transverse center index and the sight notch are aligned with a centerline marked on the workpiece before both clamp knobs are tightened, so that the pair of guided holes is placed symmetrically about the centerline. The fence controls the setback of the holes from the straight edge of the workpiece, while the two pointer readings control the hole separation and the position of the pair relative to the centerline. These three settings are made against three separate features of the jig and do not interfere with one another.

A removable spacer plate having parallel opposite faces may be fitted between the fence and the straight edge of the workpiece. The spacer plate changes the setback of every guided hole by its thickness without changing the separation between the holes, so that a second setback can be obtained without disturbing a spacing setting that has already been made.

In use, the installer selects the desired hole spacing, loosens both clamp knobs, slides the guide carriages until the pointer readings differ by the desired spacing and are centered about the transverse center index, tightens both clamp knobs, places the flat lower face on the workpiece with the fence or the installed spacer plate pressed against the selected edge, aligns the sight notch and the transverse center index with the centerline, and drills through both drill bushings. The jig is then lifted away, and no part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece.

==> draft/10-abstract.md <==
A hand drilling jig locates and guides both mounting holes of a cabinet pull in one placement. An elongated rail has a flat lower face, an upper face carrying distance marks, and a longitudinal slot. A fence held at a first end by two screws has a portion projecting below the lower face that bears against a workpiece edge; removing the screws, inverting the fence, and reinstalling them moves that portion to the opposite longitudinal side while the marked face still faces the user. Two separate guide carriages seat on the upper face, each having a key in the slot that blocks rotation while allowing sliding, a drill bushing registering with the slot, a clamp knob whose shank reaches a clamping shoe below the rail, and a pointer aligned with its bore axis. A transverse center index and an aligned sight notch register the pair on a marked centerline.

Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 3). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 (FIG. 2) are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.

The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92, as shown in FIG. 4. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90 at a right angle to that edge. Referring to FIG. 6, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. lines: Referring to FIG. 6, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.

-The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed, so that one marked face and one scale direction serve both cases and a setting already made is not lost when the reference edge changes.

+The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed.

A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 is fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.

Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key 52 (FIG. 3) that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The key 52 fits between the two long side walls of the longitudinal slot 16 and bears against them, so that the key 52 prevents the guide carriage from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the guide carriage to slide along the longitudinal slot 16.

Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing 54 (FIG. 3). The drill bushing 54 has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down the bore of the drill bushing 54 travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 holds the guide carriage against rotation and the guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.

The drill bushing 54 is a wear part. It is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of the guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing 54 whose bore has been enlarged by use, or whose bore is of a diameter other than that required for the screws of a particular pull, can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob 58 (FIG. 1) above the rail 10. A threaded shank of the clamp knob 58 passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe 60 (FIG. 3) below the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe 60 upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe 60 bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob 58 in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe 60 from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 remains below the lower face 14 and spans the longitudinal slot 16, so that it bears against the lower face 14 on each side of the longitudinal slot 16 when the clamp knob 58 is tightened and travels with the guide carriage along the rail 10 when the clamp knob 58 is loosened.

Turning the clamp knob in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. content.content:
1	In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and downward refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece. These terms are used for convenience of description and do not limit the orientation in which the jig may be used.
2	
3	Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 3). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 (FIG. 2) are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.
4	
5	The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door, a drawer front, or a like panel having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes that receive the mounting screws of a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.
6	
7	A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 is a fixed fence in the sense that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and does not slide along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below do. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92 (see FIG. 1). The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.
8	
9	Referring to FIG. 6, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.
10	
11	The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed.
12	
13	A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 is fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.
14	
15	Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are seated separately on the rail 10, one nearer to the fence 30 than the other. The two guide carriages are separate bodies. Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.
16	
17	The construction of the guide carriages is shown in FIG. 3, a cross-sectional view taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 2. The view shows the second guide carriage 70; the first guide carriage 50 is of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The first guide carriage 50 has a key 52 and the second guide carriage 70 has a like key 72 (FIG. 3). The key 52 prevents the first guide carriage 50 from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the first guide carriage 50 to slide along the longitudinal slot 16, and the key 72 does the same for the second guide carriage 70.
18	
19	Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing, a drill bushing 54 in the first guide carriage 50 and a drill bushing 74 (FIG. 3) in the second guide carriage 70. Each drill bushing has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage that carries it and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down that bore travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 and the key 72 hold their guide carriages against rotation and each guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.
20	
21	The drill bushing 54 and the drill bushing 74 are wear parts. Each is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of its guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing whose bore has been enlarged by use can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.
22	
23	Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob above the rail 10, a clamp knob 58 (FIG. 1) on the first guide carriage 50 and a clamp knob 78 (FIG. 3) on the second guide carriage 70. A threaded shank of the clamp knob passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe below the rail 10, a clamping shoe 60 in the case of the first guide carriage 50 and a clamping shoe 80 (FIG. 3) in the case of the second guide carriage 70. Turning the clamp knob in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80 each remain below the lower face 14 and bear against the lower face 14 when the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 respectively are tightened.
24	
25	The first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82, as seen in FIG. 2. The first guide carriage 50 is shown in detail in FIG. 5. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is an index feature that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.
26	
27	Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.
28	
29	Referring to FIG. 7, the rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the rail 10 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 (FIG. 7) is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, for alignment with a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 7) drawn on the workpiece 90. Sighting the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 together on the centerline 94 brings both of those features onto the centerline 94, and the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are spaced apart along the rail 10 so that the two sightings together fix the position of the jig on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92.
30	
31	The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.
32	
33	In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.
34	
35	The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.
36	
37	When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.
38	
39	The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushing 54 and the drill bushing 74 are made of hardened metal.
