file.content:
In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and downward refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece. These terms are used for convenience of description and do not limit the orientation in which the jig may be used.

Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 3). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 (FIG. 2) are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.

The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door, a drawer front, or a like panel having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes that receive the mounting screws of a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.

A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 is a fixed fence in the sense that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and does not slide along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below do. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that extends below the lower face 14 and bears against the workpiece edge 92 (see FIG. 1). The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.

Referring to FIG. 6, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. Removing the two screws 34, turning the fence 30 over, and reinstalling the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36 places the fence 30 in a second orientation, in which the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.

The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed.

A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes or the alignment of the rail 10 with respect to the workpiece edge 92. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 is fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92, and it is removed by lifting it away from the fence 30.

Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are seated separately on the rail 10, one nearer to the fence 30 than the other. The two guide carriages are separate bodies. Neither guide carriage is coupled to the other, and each is positioned along the rail 10 independently of the other.

The construction of the guide carriages is shown in FIG. 3, a cross-sectional view taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 2. The view shows the second guide carriage 70; the first guide carriage 50 is of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The first guide carriage 50 has a key 52 and the second guide carriage 70 has a like key 72 (FIG. 3). The key 52 prevents the first guide carriage 50 from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the first guide carriage 50 to slide along the longitudinal slot 16, and the key 72 does the same for the second guide carriage 70.

Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing, a drill bushing 54 in the first guide carriage 50 and a drill bushing 74 (FIG. 3) in the second guide carriage 70. Each drill bushing has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage that carries it and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down that bore travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 and the key 72 hold their guide carriages against rotation and each guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.

The drill bushing 54 and the drill bushing 74 are wear parts. Each is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of its guide carriage as a separate piece, so that a drill bushing whose bore has been enlarged by use can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced.

Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob above the rail 10, a clamp knob 58 (FIG. 1) on the first guide carriage 50 and a clamp knob 78 (FIG. 3) on the second guide carriage 70. A threaded shank of the clamp knob passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe below the rail 10, a clamping shoe 60 in the case of the first guide carriage 50 and a clamping shoe 80 (FIG. 3) in the case of the second guide carriage 70. Turning the clamp knob in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80 each remain below the lower face 14 and bear against the lower face 14 when the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 respectively are tightened.

The first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82, as seen in FIG. 2. The first guide carriage 50 is shown in detail in FIG. 5. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is an index feature that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.

Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. A misreading or a misplacement of one guide carriage displaces only the hole guided by that guide carriage and is not carried into the position of the other hole, unlike an arrangement in which one position is set from a scale and the second position is then measured from the first.

Referring to FIG. 7, the rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the rail 10 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 (FIG. 7) is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, for alignment with a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 7) drawn on the workpiece 90. Sighting the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 together on the centerline 94 brings both of those features onto the centerline 94, and the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are spaced apart along the rail 10 so that the two sightings together fix the position of the jig on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92.

The three settings that the jig makes are separate from one another and are made against separate features. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair along the rail 10. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26, sighted together on the centerline 94, set the position of the pair on the workpiece 90 in the direction along the workpiece edge 92. Changing one of the three settings does not disturb the other two.

In use, the user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.

The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which squares the rail 10 to that edge and fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.

When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.

The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushing 54 and the drill bushing 74 are made of hardened metal.

The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

3:Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 3). A straight longitudinal slot 16 runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 (FIG. 2) are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.
17:The construction of the guide carriages is shown in FIG. 3, a cross-sectional view taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 2 through the second guide carriage 70, and in FIG. 5, a cross-sectional view taken on line 5-5 of FIG. 2 through the first guide carriage 50. The two guide carriages are of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The first guide carriage 50 has a key 52 (FIG. 5) and the second guide carriage 70 has a like key 72 (FIG. 3). The key 52 prevents the first guide carriage 50 from rotating relative to the rail 10 while allowing the first guide carriage 50 to slide along the longitudinal slot 16, and the key 72 does the same for the second guide carriage 70.
19:Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing, a drill bushing 54 (FIG. 5) in the first guide carriage 50 and a drill bushing 74 (FIG. 3) in the second guide carriage 70. Each drill bushing has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage that carries it and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down that bore travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. Because the key 52 and the key 72 hold their guide carriages against rotation and each guide carriage seats flat on the upper face 12, the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and each hole is therefore started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.
23:Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob above the rail 10, a clamp knob 58 (FIG. 1) on the first guide carriage 50 and a clamp knob 78 (FIG. 3) on the second guide carriage 70. A threaded shank of the clamp knob passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe below the rail 10, a clamping shoe 60 (FIG. 5) in the case of the first guide carriage 50 and a clamping shoe 80 (FIG. 3) in the case of the second guide carriage 70. Turning the clamp knob in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe from the lower face 14 and allows the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80 each remain below the lower face 14 and bear against the lower face 14 when the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 respectively are tightened.

input.summary: Resumed the filing repair and worked every blocker in the previous QA report. Removed the untraced matter (clamping shoe spanning the slot, key bearing on the slot side walls, bushings of differing bore diameter, sight-notch runout and visibility, the "right angle to the straight edge" relationship, the second-workpiece method claim, the closing-paragraph variants, printed pointers, and the extra negative limitations about fasteners and power sources), so that every remaining statement traces to a sentence of input/disclosure.md. Cancelled two method claims and renumbered to a consecutive 1 to 22 with valid dependencies. Split the shared reference numerals so each numbered part means one thing: the second guide carriage now has key 72, drill bushing 74, clamp knob 78 and clamping shoe 80. Because a numeral used in the description must also appear in the drawings, FIG. 5 was converted from a top plan detail into a cross-sectional view on line 5-5 of FIG. 2 through the first guide carriage, which is where key 52, drill bushing 54, clamp knob 58 and clamping shoe 60 are now shown; FIG. 2 carries both cutting-plane lines with endpoints, alignment and arrow directions stated. Figure citations in the description now match the sheets (the centering features cite FIG. 7, the fence bearing directly on the edge cites FIG. 1, both carriage sections are cited), and the article is called a drilling jig everywhere including the Brief Description and the figure briefs. One point of disagreement with the report: it suggested keeping FIG. 5 as a top plan detail of the first guide carriage, which would have left numerals 52 and 60 in the text but on no sheet; I applied the numeral split it asked for and moved that sheet to a section instead, which satisfies both requirements. Note on prior art: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the Background contains no citations and the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
reasoning: Claim 1 keeps only what the disclosure states and what does the technical work: a rail with a slot and marks, a two-screw fence that inverts to move the projecting portion from one longitudinal side of the rail to the other while the marked face keeps facing the user, and two mutually uncoupled carriages each with its own key, bushing, clamp knob and shoe, each carrying its own pointer read against the same marks. The reversible-fence-plus-two-independent-readings combination is the feature that carries the claim; no reference was supplied to write around, so nothing was added to claim 1 for that purpose.

Deleted 'bearing against side walls of the longitudinal slot' from the key limitation of claim 1. The disclosure gives the key's function (anti-rotation while sliding) but never a contact topology with the slot walls, and an unsupported limitation in claim 1 is scope given away as well as a fidelity defect. The functional recitation is what the description now supports word for word.

Claim 6 was rewritten to recite only that the sight notch and the center index are spaced apart along the rail and are alignable together with a marked centerline. Where the notch runs out, which end position it occupies, and whether the centerline is visible through it are geometry the inventor never supplied, and for a functional sight surface those statements are substantive rather than a drawing convention.

Claim 12 now recites the shoe as disposed below the lower face and bearing on it when tightened. The disclosure says the shank passes through the slot into a shoe below the rail and the rail is clamped between carriage and shoe; it does not say the shoe spans the slot or bears on each side of it, so the fallback claim was narrowed to the disclosed relationship rather than deleted.

Cancelled the method claim to bushings of a different bore diameter and the method claim to drilling a second workpiece from an opposite-side edge. The disclosure supports replaceable hardened-metal bushings but says nothing about diameters, and its reversal teaching is about which edge of a workpiece is referenced, not about carrying a setting across to a second panel. Both were dependent claims, so the ladder still runs from the parallel-and-perpendicular bores through the spacer plate, the reversible mounting, the replaceable bushings, the anti-rotation result during drilling, and the hand-operated no-power condition.

Removed 'at a right angle to that edge' from the description and from claims 13 and 18. The source says the fence is perpendicular to the rail and that the rail extends inward across the workpiece; the added relationship also fought the draft's own reversible-fence structure and the Background premise that both holes share one setback, so the disclosed wording was restored.

Split the duplicated carriage numerals instead of keeping one numeral for each pair of identical parts. That forced a drawing decision: with the second carriage's parts on the FIG. 3 section, the first carriage's key and shoe would have appeared in the text and on no sheet. Converting FIG. 5 to a section on line 5-5 through the first carriage puts every numeral on a sheet and keeps each sheet at eight numerals or fewer.

FIG. 7 now states only the disclosed alignment: the index runs across the band transverse to the rail, the notch is formed in the second end and aligned with the index, and the centerline is a line on the workpiece aligned with both. The centerline's direction relative to the rail, its passage through the slot, and its meeting point with the index were drawing-driven geometry with no source behind them.

Left ¶37 alone. Its statement that the carriage settings and the reading direction survive a fence reversal is the same relationship the report expressly preserved in ¶11 through its own suggested wording, and it follows from the disclosed structure that reversing the fence touches only the two screws.
